rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A kasra on bāʾ yields biyūt beside buyūt as a dialectal broken-plural pattern, with no change in meaning.
rows.anchor: ḍamma to kasra on bāʾ; dialectal variation in broken plural pattern

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Assimilation merges the two tāʾs into a doubled dhāl; the heavier sound emphasizes remembrance without changing the meaning.
rows.anchor: Full assimilation variant: both tāʾs merge into dhāl with shaddah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This reading retains and writes the root-final hamza explicitly in huzuʾan.
rows.anchor: Hamza retained explicitly in spelling: huzuʾan — preserves the root-final hamza in orthography

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With sukūn on zāy, huzʾan drops the medial vowel and compresses the pronunciation into one syllable.
rows.anchor: Sukūn on zāy with hamza: huzʾan — compressed pronunciation dropping the medial vowel

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second hamza is softened between vowels, a pronunciation identified as common in Ḥijāzī recitation.
rows.anchor: Hamza softened (tashīl) — the second hamza in raʾayta is eased between vowels

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A canonical variant elides the second hamza entirely to simplify the consonant cluster.
rows.anchor: Hamza dropped entirely — the second hamza is elided, simplifying the consonant cluster

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This variant inserts a lengthened alif before the hamza as compensatory elongation.
rows.anchor: Madd (elongation) inserted — a lengthened alif before the hamza; compensatory lengthening variant

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reading explicitly retains the full first-person yāʾ, lengthening the final syllable without changing meaning.
rows.anchor: Full yāʾ al-mutakallim explicitly written — no semantic change but prosodic lengthening

rows.speaker: Qālūn, Ibn Kathīr
rows.claim: Shortening the final alif yields ana rather than anā; Qālūn and Ibn Kathīr are given as examples, with no semantic change but altered cadence.
rows.anchor: Canonical within the seven readings (e.g., Qālūn, Ibn Kathīr). The shortening does not alter meaning

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The full first-person yāʾ makes the I phonetically prominent through a longer final syllable, with no semantic change.
rows.anchor: Full yāʾ al-mutakallim explicitly written — no semantic change but prosodic lengthening of final syllable

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Adding the final yāʾ gives a fuller first-person pronoun form and lengthens the ending.
rows.anchor: Addition of final yāʾ to the first-person pronoun — wa-aṭīʿūnī with long ī

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The added final yāʾ restores the fuller -nī pronoun form and lengthens the ending.
rows.anchor: Addition of final yāʾ to the first-person pronoun — wa-aṭīʿūnī with long ī at end

rows.speaker: Ḥafṣ
rows.claim: The standard Ḥafṣ form is a passive participle from Form IV kh-r-j, and the source says it is universal across major transmissions.
rows.anchor: standard Hafs reading — passive participle Form IV kh-r-j (mukhraj from ʾakhraja)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The final yāʾ restores the fuller pronoun and, in the Aykah context, underscores Shuʿayb’s personal authority: obey me.
rows.anchor: in the Aykah context, the fuller form intensifies the personal specificity of the messenger's authority claim

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The variant fa-tawakkal uses causal fāʾ for therefore, presenting trust as a consequence; wa-tawakkal coordinates it with what precedes.
rows.anchor: fāʾ al-sababiyya replaces wāw al-ʿaṭf; ""therefore put your trust"" (consequence) vs

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A pausal hāʾ is added after interrogative mā; it marks a pause without changing meaning and confirms that mā is interrogative, not relative.
rows.anchor: Pausal hāʾ added to mā after bāʾ — bimah vs bima; hāʾ al-sakt marks pause

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This canonical form keeps the full yāʾ on the first-person pronoun, extending the ending without changing meaning.
rows.anchor: Canonical reading with full yāʾ on pronoun — extended first-person singular ending

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At pause, the canonical variant may drop or retain the yāʾ according to dialectal pausal convention.
rows.anchor: Canonical variant with pause form dropping yāʾ or retaining it — dialectal pause conventions

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Assimilation merges nūn al-wiqāya into the following nūn as a phonological simplification.
rows.anchor: Canonical variant with assimilation of nūn al-wiqāya into the following nūn

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This shortened pronoun form drops the final yāʾ while keeping the same meaning, as a dialectal pause form.
rows.anchor: Canonical variant with shortened pronoun — drops final yāʾ; same meaning

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The canonical variants allow a full yāʾ, deleted yāʾ, or fatḥa on the yāʾ.
rows.anchor: Canonical variants with three phonological options — full yāʾ, deleted yāʾ, or fatḥa on yāʾ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This pair distinguishes the pausal form ātān from the connected form ātāniya.
rows.anchor: Canonical variant pair — pause form (ātān) and connected form (ātāniya)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Among the ten readings, the form has either a full yāʾ or a fatḥa-yāʾ, with no semantic difference.
rows.anchor: Ten-reading canonical — full yāʾ or fatḥa-yāʾ; no semantic difference

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ten-reading variant permits either the long or short pronoun ending.
rows.anchor: Ten-reading canonical — long or short pronoun ending

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ḥuzn form shifts the vowel pattern from ḥazan to another attested maṣdar pattern; both mean grief or sorrow, reflecting dialectal morphology.
rows.anchor: Both ḥazan and ḥuzn are attested gerunds of h-z-n with essentially identical meaning

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The canonical ten-reader form drops hamza from khāṭiʾīn with vowel compensation; the dominant analysis keeps the sense sinners.
rows.anchor: Hamza-drop variant: khāṭiʾīn → khāṭīn, elision of the hamza with vowel compensation. Canonical within the ten readings.

rows.speaker: some grammarians
rows.claim: Some grammarians suggest a possible derivation from khaṭā, to step or walk, yielding those who tread; the source says the dominant reading remains a pronunciation variant meaning sinners.
rows.anchor: Some grammarians note this could theoretically derive from a different root (khaṭā ""to step, walk"") meaning

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A canonical u-vowel form varies the Form I imperfect dialectally; both forms mean violent seizure, though some grammatical analyses hear greater emphasis in the ḍamma form.
rows.anchor: Vowel shift i→u on the middle radical (fatḥa→ḍamma on the stem)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The explicit final yāʾ with fatḥa realizes the first-person suffix without changing its root, meaning, or parsing.
rows.anchor: Variant spells out the 1cs pronoun ya explicitly (fatḥah on final yāʾ instead of elision/sukūn)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ishmām blends a trace of the active ḍamma with the passive kasra on qāf, signaling the underlying active form while retaining passive morphology.
rows.anchor: the qāf receives a combined ḍamma-kasra (ishmām), blending the passive-voice kasra with a trace

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fatḥa on the final yāʾ gives ʿindiya rather than ʿindī; it is a dialectal pronunciation difference with no meaning change.
rows.anchor: Variant with fatḥa on final yāʾ (ʿindiya instead of ʿindī) — a phonological variation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A ten-reader variant removes hamza and replaces it with yāʾ, reflecting dialectal hamza avoidance without semantic change.
rows.anchor: Hamza removal: fiʾatin→fiyatin; canonical 10-reader variant; hamza replaced by yāʾ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The active reading means you return rather than you are returned, giving the addressees agency in their return.
rows.anchor: Active voice reading: ""you return"" instead of passive ""you are returned"" — grants agency to the addressees

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This variant changes the realization of the interrogative hamza without changing the meaning.
rows.anchor: Hamza treatment variant — alternative realization of the interrogative hamza, no semantic change

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third-person plural passive changes the address from you to they and presents return as a universal cosmic principle.
rows.anchor: Third-person masculine plural passive — shifts addressee from ""you"" to ""they,"" universalizing the return

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third-person plural active means they return voluntarily, removing passive compulsion and assigning agency to the subjects.
rows.anchor: Third-person masculine plural active — ""they return"" voluntarily, removing passive compulsion; subjects have agency

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second-person plural active means you return voluntarily, preserving direct address while assigning human agency.
rows.anchor: Second-person masculine plural active — ""you return"" voluntarily, preserving direct address but granting human agency

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kasra rather than fatḥa on the final yāʾ shifts the form from accusative or vocative toward genitive or possessive emphasis.
rows.anchor: Kasra on final yāʾ instead of fatḥa — shifts from accusative/vocative to genitive/possessive emphasis

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The accusative al-baḥra can be parsed as object of an omitted verb or coordinated with the ism of anna, keeping the sea within the original clause.
rows.anchor: Accusative reading (naṣb): al-baḥra as object of a deleted verb or maʿṭūf on ism anna

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The active Form I means you yourselves return, unlike the standard passive you are returned, shifting agency to the subjects.
rows.anchor: Active voice Form I (tarjiʿūna): ""you [yourselves] return"" — vs. standard passive turjaʿūna

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The single-zāy Form I variant may mean became mighty or overcame, and transitively We overpowered or made rare; it shifts from intensive reinforcement to simple strengthening.
rows.anchor: Canonical variant with single zāy (Form I: 'azaza instead of Form II: 'azzaza)

rows.speaker: Yaʿqūb
rows.claim: A Yaʿqūb-style performance preserves a hādī-like form before pause or continuation while the standard surface has hādin, affecting final-glide and pause texture.
rows.anchor: Canonical Ya'qub-style performance preserves a hādī-like form before pause/continuation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Vowel harmony gives qīla a rounded transitional vowel after wāw while retaining the passive q-w-l form.
rows.anchor: Canonical vowel-harmony reading gives qīla a rounded transitional vowel after wa

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural reading changes His servant to His servants, broadening the claim of sufficiency from one servant to the servant community.
rows.anchor: Canonical plural reading changes singular His servant to His servants, broadening the sufficiency claim

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pause or continuation variant permits final yāʾ realization at a recitation boundary while preserving the active participle.
rows.anchor: Canonical pause/continuation variant preserves the active participle while allowing final yāʾ realization

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Vowel harmony changes the passive vocalic texture but leaves the consonantal verb and procession meaning unchanged.
rows.anchor: Canonical vowel-harmony variant colors the passive vocalic texture while preserving the same consonantal verb

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The doubled reading intensifies the opening, suggesting repeated or multiple gate access, or an emphatically activated opening.
rows.anchor: Canonical doubled reading intensifies the opening, suggesting repeated, multiple, or emphatically activated gate access

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Opening the final yāʾ as -iya makes the first-person suffix fuller in recitation without changing root or syntax.
rows.anchor: Final yāʾ is opened as -iya, making the first-person suffix more fully vocalized

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Opening the final yāʾ as -iya gives a fuller recitation of the first-person suffix without syntactic change.
rows.anchor: Final yāʾ is opened as -iya, making the first-person suffix fuller in recitation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The variant wa-an coordinates the two feared outcomes conjunctively instead of linking them disjunctively with aw-an.
rows.anchor: Canonical variant replaces aw an with wa-an, coordinating both feared outcomes conjunctively rather than disjunctively

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The variant makes corruption a nominative subject of an intransitive verb meaning to appear in the land.
rows.anchor: Canonical variant makes corruption nominative subject of intransitive appearance in the land

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sukūn on sīn compresses rusulukum to ruslukum, tightening the sound while preserving referent and syntactic role.
rows.anchor: Canonical sukūn reading compresses the plural from rusulukum to ruslukum

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Form IV variant is a simpler causative sending-down; Form II can suggest staged or intensive descent, though both mean causing descent.
rows.anchor: Canonical variant reads Form IV instead of Form II; both mean causing descent

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The standard Form II with shadda marks repeated, intensified, or staged causative descent of rain.
rows.anchor: Canonical standard line vocalizes Form II with shadda, marking repeated, intensified, or staged causative descent

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Form IV without shadda presents the rain’s descent as caused sending-down with less overt staging force.
rows.anchor: Canonical variant reads Form IV without shadda, presenting the rain's descent as caused sending-down

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The imperative’s internal vowel shifts from i to u, preserving the root and command force.
rows.anchor: Canonical vowel variant changes the internal vowel from i to u in the imperative

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The vowel variant changes inna-ka to anna-ka, permitting a more subordinating or object-like clause link.
rows.anchor: Canonical vowel variant changes إِنَّكَ (innaka) to أَنَّكَ (annaka), allowing a more subordinating

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Assimilation of the Form VI prefix tāʾ into lām is phonetic and does not change meaning.
rows.anchor: Assimilation of tāʾ — phonetic variant, no semantic change; the tāʾ of the Form VI prefix

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dropping the hamza of raʾā facilitates pronunciation while leaving the grammar unchanged.
rows.anchor: Hamza of raʾā dropped entirely (tashīl) — phonological facilitation; grammatically identical to standard

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hamza is lengthened into ā by madd badal, adding emphatic stretch and rhetorical weight to the question.
rows.anchor: Hamza prolonged into long ā vowel (madd badal) — emphatic stretching of the interrogative

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This dialectal variant realizes the hamza as a transitional glottal stop between full hamza and elision.
rows.anchor: Hamza realized as transitional glottal stop — intermediate between full hamza and complete elision

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Softening replaces the final hamza with long ā without changing meaning, and makes the word ending less abrupt.
rows.anchor: final hamza of yunabbaʾ replaced by long ā — phonetic variant without semantic change

rows.speaker: Ibn Kathīr and others
rows.claim: Ibn Kathīr and other readers drop or soften the hamza in qurʾān to qurān; the source describes this as standard Ḥijāzī practice.
rows.anchor: attested in the reading of Ibn Kathīr and others. This softening of the hamza was standard Ḥijāzī practice

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sukūn on sīn lightens the broken plural by reducing its medial vowel.
rows.anchor: Sukūn on sīn — lightened pronunciation of the broken plural, reducing the medial vowel

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Assimilation merges the final nūn into wāw incompletely, carrying its nasal into the oath particle.
rows.anchor: Assimilation of nūn's final consonant into the wāw — idghām nāqiṣ, merging the nasal

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The qibal form shifts the sense from temporal before him to spatial facing him or in his presence.
rows.anchor: Vowel shift qabl→qibal changes meaning from ""before him"" (temporal) to ""facing him / in his presence""

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Softening hamza to yāʾ is phonological and does not change meaning.
rows.anchor: Hamzah softened to yāʾ — phonological variant without semantic change

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The source identifies tanwīn as the standard reading of tadhkiratan.
rows.anchor: Standard reading with tanwīn

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sukūn on dhāl gives the lighter udhn form; both forms are canonical and carry the same meaning.
rows.anchor: Sukūn on dhāl — lighter form (udhun vs udhn), both canonical; no semantic difference

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The canonical ten variants permit forms with or without full hāʾ al-sakt, allowing variation in the trailing vowel.
rows.anchor: Canonical ten variant allowing both forms — with and without full hāʾ al-sakt

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The standard Form IV perfect aghnā means availed or sufficed.
rows.anchor: Standard reading: Form IV perfect, ""availed/sufficed""

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The standard reading pauses with saktah on the hāʾ of māliyah before halaka in 69:29; the hāʾ marks the possessive suffix at pause.
rows.anchor: Standard reading with saktah: pause on hāʾ of māliyah before halaka (69:29)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Without the pausal hāʾ, māliya runs directly into halaka; -ya remains the first-person possessive suffix.
rows.anchor: Without pausal hāʾ: māliya runs directly into halaka; -ya is the 1sg possessive suffix

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Assimilation merges the hāʾ at the end of māliyah into the initial hāʾ of halaka in continuous recitation.
rows.anchor: Assimilation: hāʾ of māliyah assimilates into hāʾ of halaka — continuous articulation merging the two words
